title: Camp Two: three peaks and the token shop
summary: Two of the sprint's puzzle peaks come back to be taught to the family, then one climb each over multi-step equations, break-even and proportions, and the month 2 monster gets its ending.
materials: the field journal, open at the sprint's puzzle pages
your cost sheet, your price table and your tags, to hold beside the summit numbers afterwards
the expedition wall map, for planting the second flag

steps.title: The climb, in order
steps.body:
Camp Two is not a test. It is the second flat place on the mountain, and the view backwards is longer than it was at Camp One.

Today runs in three parts. First, two of the sprint's peaks come back: one that is cracked by splitting into cases, and one that is cracked by painting a board. You solve them, and then you gather the family and teach the problem you invented in week 7. Teaching is the hardest way to find out whether you actually own something.

Then the summit: three peaks, one for each week of the sprint. Peak 1 is multi-step equations with the letter sitting in both pans. Peak 2 is break-even and profit. Peak 3 is proportions, unit cost and percent. Every one of them is written with suppose numbers instead of yours, so a wrong answer today costs you nothing. When the three peaks are climbed, put your own cost sheet and your own tags on the table and run the same three questions on your real numbers. That is the part that matters at the stand.

Last, the month 2 monster, the token shop, either gets cracked or gets retired with honours. Both endings are respectable. Only pretending counts as failing.

steps.title: Two peaks from the sprint, back for teaching

problems.prompt: How many three-digit whole numbers have digits that add up to 4?
explanation: A three-digit number's first digit is at least 1, and since the three digits add to only 4, it cannot be more than 4 either.
That is four cases, no fifth.
First digit 1 leaves 3 to split between the other two digits, which happens four ways.
First digit 2 leaves 2, shared three ways. First digit 3 leaves 1, shared two ways. First digit 4 leaves 0, shared one way.
The cases cannot overlap, since a number has exactly one first digit, so add them: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 is 10.
Splitting into cases tells you the count before you write a single number down.
problems.useAgain: when a count has a restriction inside it, and sorting every possibility into cases is safer than listing them.
hints: One of the three digits is not free to be anything at all. Which one, and why does that turn this into a splitting job?
Fix the first digit at 1 and count how many ways the other two digits can hold what is left over. Then do the same for the next first digit.
problems.socraticHint: How large is the first digit allowed to get here, and what does that tell you about how many cases there are before you open any of them?

variant.prompt: How many three-digit whole numbers have digits that add up to 5?

problems.prompt: A chessboard has 64 squares, 32 dark and 32 light, and squares that touch are always different colours. Two opposite corners are cut off, and those two corners are the same colour as each other, leaving 62 squares. A domino covers exactly two squares that touch. True or false: 31 dominoes can cover the 62 remaining squares with no gaps and no overlaps.
explanation: Every domino lies across two touching squares, and touching squares are never the same colour.
So one domino always covers one dark and one light square, however it is placed.
Thirty-one dominoes would therefore cover 31 dark squares and 31 light squares, whatever pattern anyone arranges them in.
The two cut corners were the same colour as each other, so one colour lost two squares and the other lost none.
That leaves 30 squares of one colour and 32 of the other.
Thirty-one and thirty-one cannot be thirty and thirty-two, so no arrangement exists, and painting the board settled it without moving a single domino.
problems.useAgain: when a covering or a tiling looks impossible and you want a reason instead of a tired hand.
hints: Nobody wins this by sliding dominoes around. Look at the colours before you look at the shapes.
Work out how many squares of each colour a single domino has to cover, then count how many of each colour the cut board actually has left.
problems.socraticHint: Two opposite corners of a chessboard: are they the same colour as each other, and why would a domino care?

variant.prompt: A 5 by 5 board is coloured like a chessboard, so it holds 13 squares of the corner colour and 12 of the other. One corner square is cut off, leaving 24 squares. True or false: 12 dominoes can cover the 24 remaining squares with no gaps and no overlaps.

steps.title: Teach the family the problem you invented
steps.prompt:
Gather the family at the whiteboard and teach the problem you invented in week 7: the board or shape you chose, the piece, the colouring, and the claim you proved by counting colours instead of squares.

Teach it the way it was cracked, not the way it was written down. Colour the board in front of them first, then ask them what your piece is always forced to cover, and only then reveal your claim. Let them try to find an arrangement that breaks it before you show them why counting colours already ruled it out.

One rule for teaching: never say a number until they have wanted it. Ask, wait, and let the answer be theirs. Finish by asking whether anyone can break it, and answer whatever they throw at you.

problems.prompt: Peak 1, the cost formula. Suppose a cost sheet says that making n units costs total = 12 + 3n dollars: 12 dollars that gets spent once whatever happens, and 3 dollars more for every unit made. Suppose the total came to 42 dollars. How many units is that?
explanation: The 12 dollars is spent once and does not care how many units there are, so take it off the total first: 42 less 12 leaves 30 dollars.
That 30 dollars is the part that grew unit by unit, and each unit added 3 dollars to it.
So the equation is 3n = 30, and splitting both pans into three equal shares gives n = 10 units.
Walk it forwards to check: 10 units at 3 dollars is 30, plus the 12 that was spent once, is 42.
problems.useAgain: when a total is built from one cost that happens once plus one cost that happens every time, and you want the count.
hints: One of those two numbers does not care how many units were made. Deal with that one before you touch the other.
Take the once-only cost off both sides first, and see what the equation says about the part that grew.
problems.socraticHint: Which piece of that total would still have been paid if no units at all had been made?

variant.prompt: Suppose a cost sheet says total = 15 + 4n dollars, and the total came to 59 dollars. How many units is that?

problems.prompt: Peak 1, the letter on both sides. Suppose there are two ways to make the same thing. Way A costs 20 dollars to set up and 4 dollars for every unit after that. Way B costs 32 dollars to set up and 2 dollars for every unit after that. At how many units do the two ways cost exactly the same?
explanation: Write both ways in the same letter: way A is 20 + 4n, and way B is 32 + 2n.
They are equal where 20 + 4n = 32 + 2n.
The letter sits in both pans, so clean one pan first: take 2n off both sides to get 20 + 2n = 32.
Take 20 off both sides to get 2n = 12, then halve both sides to get n = 6 units.
Check both ways at 6 units: 20 plus 24 is 44, and 32 plus 12 is 44.
Below 6 units way A is cheaper, since its setup is smaller; above 6 units way B is cheaper.
problems.useAgain: when two different plans grow at different rates and you want the count where they meet.
hints: Write each way as its own expression first, in the same letter, before you write any equals sign at all.
The letter is in both pans. Take the smaller pile of letters off both sides and see what is left.
problems.socraticHint: Which of the two ways is cheaper when almost nothing is made, and does that stay true forever?

variant.prompt: Way A costs 9 dollars to set up and 5 dollars for every unit after that. Way B costs 24 dollars to set up and 2 dollars for every unit after that. At how many units do the two ways cost exactly the same?

problems.prompt: Three of these four equations are solved by n = 4. One of them is not. Which one?
explanation: The fastest test is to put 4 in and see whether both sides agree, since a solution is a number that makes them match.
In the first, 5 fours less 3 is 17, and 2 fours plus 9 is also 17.
In the second, 7 fours is 28, matching 4 fours plus 12.
In the third, 2 lots of 9 is 18, matching 3 fours plus 6.
In the last, 6 fours less 2 is 22, but 4 fours plus 10 is 26, so 4 is not its solution.
Solving it properly gives n = 6, but testing the handed number is faster than solving all four from scratch.
problems.useAgain: when you are handed a candidate answer and want to know which equations it really fits.
hints: You do not have to solve four equations. You were handed a number, so use it.
Put 4 in place of n in one equation at a time and work each side out separately before comparing them.
problems.socraticHint: What does it actually mean to say that a number solves an equation, and how could that meaning save you three solvings?

variant.prompt: Three of these four equations are solved by n = 3. One of them is not. Which one?

problems.prompt: Peak 1 summit. Solve 4(n + 3) = 2(n + 11) - 6. What is n?
explanation: Open both brackets first, spreading each number across everything inside its own bracket. The left side becomes 4n + 12, and 2 lots of (n + 11) is 2n + 22.
The right side still has the 6 to take away: 2n + 22 less 6 is 2n + 16. So the equation reads 4n + 12 = 2n + 16.
The letter is in both pans, so clean the smaller one. Take 2n off both sides: 2n + 12 = 16.
Take 12 off both sides: 2n = 4. Halve both sides: n = 2.
Walk it forwards to check: 4 lots of 5 is 20, and 2 lots of 13 less 6 is also 20. It balances.
problems.useAgain: when an equation hides its letter inside brackets on both sides and the brackets have to be opened first.
hints: Nothing can be compared while the brackets are shut. Open both of them before you move anything across.
On the right, open the bracket before you deal with the 6 being taken away, then gather that whole side into two pieces.
problems.socraticHint: Once both brackets are open, how many n pieces does each side hold, and which side is holding fewer?

problems.prompt: Peak 2, break-even. Suppose a stand has 18 dollars of costs that happen once whatever happens, each unit costs 2 dollars to make, and each unit sells for 5 dollars. Which equation says that after n units are sold the money taken in exactly equals the money paid out?
explanation: Money taken in is the price times the number sold, which is 5n. Nothing else comes in.
Money paid out has two parts living in different pockets: the 18 dollars that happens once, and 2 dollars for each of the n units, which is 2n. So money out is 18 + 2n.
Break-even is the count where those two are equal, so the equation is 5n = 18 + 2n.

Each of the other three moves a number into the wrong pocket. One puts the price and the making cost on the same side. One multiplies the once-only cost by n, as though it were paid for every unit. One adds the money taken in to the costs.
problems.useAgain: when a shop's costs and price have to become one equation before anything can be solved.
hints: Write the two sides in words first, money in and money out, and only then look at the options.
Ask which of these numbers happens once and which happens for every single unit, then check whether each option keeps them apart.
problems.socraticHint: If nothing at all had sold, which of these costs would still have been paid?

variant.prompt: Suppose a stand has 24 dollars of costs that happen once, each unit costs 3 dollars to make, and each unit sells for 7 dollars. Which equation says that after n units the money taken in exactly equals the money paid out?

problems.prompt: Peak 2, profit as an inequality. The same stand: 18 dollars of costs that happen once, 2 dollars to make each unit, and 5 dollars a unit to buy. Profit is money in less money out. What is the smallest whole number of units sold for which the profit is greater than zero?
explanation: Write profit as one expression before asking anything about it: money in less money out is 5n less (18 + 2n).
Take the bracket away carefully, since everything inside it is being paid out: 5n less 18 less 2n, which gathers into 3n less 18.
Profit greater than zero means 3n less 18 is greater than 0, so 3n is greater than 18, so n is greater than 6.
Greater than 6 is not the same as 6. At exactly 6 units the profit is 0, which is break-even, not profit. The smallest whole number bigger than 6 is 7.
The trap is answering with the break-even count. Break-even is where profit starts, and the question asked where it is already there.
problems.useAgain: when a question asks for more than zero rather than exactly zero, and the answer has to step past the crossing point.
hints: Build one expression for profit first, and keep the paid-out part inside a bracket until you are ready to open it.
Say what profit greater than zero means about that expression, then tidy it the way you would tidy an equation.
problems.socraticHint: What exactly is the profit at the break-even count, and does that count as profit?

variant.prompt: A stand has 20 dollars of costs that happen once, 3 dollars to make each unit, and sells each unit for 7 dollars. What is the smallest whole number of units sold for which the profit is greater than zero?

problems.prompt: Peak 2 summit. Suppose a stand has 18 dollars of costs that happen once and 2 dollars of cost for each unit made. Suppose 14 units are made and all 14 sell, and the profit at the end is meant to be exactly 24 dollars. What must one unit sell for?
explanation: Work out everything that is paid out first, because none of it depends on the price. The once-only cost is 18 dollars, and 14 units at 2 dollars each is 28 dollars, so 46 dollars goes out.
Profit is what is left after every cost is paid. For 24 dollars to be left, the money taken in has to be 46 with 24 more, which is 70 dollars.
That 70 dollars comes in as 14 equal sales, so 14p = 70 and p = 5.00 dollars.
Check it forwards: 14 sales at 5 dollars is 70 in, 46 out, and 24 left over. The loan and the profit both live in that last number, which is why week 9 counts it by hand.
problems.useAgain: when you know the profit you are aiming at and have to work backwards through the costs to a price.
hints: Nothing about the costs depends on the price, so total them up before you think about price at all.
Ask what the money taken in would have to be for that much to be left over, then share it across the sales.
problems.socraticHint: Is the money taken in the same thing as the money made, and which of those two did the question aim at?

variant.prompt: A stand has 30 dollars of costs that happen once and 4 dollars of cost for each unit made. Suppose 10 units are made and all 10 sell, and the profit is meant to be exactly 20 dollars. What must one unit sell for?

problems.prompt: Peak 3, scaling the recipe. Suppose making 6 units uses 21 meters of cord, and every unit uses the same amount. How many meters of cord does making 16 units use?
explanation: Two ratios in balance make an equation: 21 meters go with 6 units the same way that an unknown number of meters goes with 16 units.
The easiest legal move is to find one unit first. Twenty-one meters shared between 6 units is 3.5 meters inside each unit.
Sixteen units at 3.5 meters each is 56 meters.
Sense check before you write it down. Sixteen units is more than twice 6 units and less than three times it. So the answer had to land between 42 and 63 meters, and 56 sits where it should.
problems.useAgain: when a recipe is known for one batch size and you need it for a different batch at the same rate.
hints: Sixteen is not a whole number of times bigger than 6, so doubling and patching will get messy. Find something smaller to build from.
Work out how much cord sits inside a single unit first, then build the bigger batch out of that.
problems.socraticHint: Sixteen units is somewhere between twice and three times six units. What does that tell you about the answer before you calculate anything?

variant.prompt: Suppose making 8 units uses 20 meters of cord, and every unit uses the same amount. How many meters does making 14 units use?

problems.prompt: Peak 3, the markup. Suppose one unit costs 8 dollars to make, and the tag price is set by adding a markup of 25 percent of that cost. What does the tag say?
explanation: Percent means per hundred, so 25 percent is 25 out of every 100, which is a quarter.
The markup is a quarter of the cost, and a quarter of 8 dollars is 2 dollars.
The tag is the cost with the markup added on top: 8 dollars with 2 dollars more is 10.00 dollars.

Be careful about what the percent is measured against. Here it is a percent of the cost, so it is the 8 that gets quartered. A percent of the tag would be a different question with a different answer.
problems.useAgain: when a price is built by adding a percent of the cost on top of the cost.
hints: Turn 25 percent into a simpler fraction before you multiply anything.
Work the markup out on its own first, as a number of dollars, and only then decide what to do with it.
problems.socraticHint: Twenty-five percent of what, exactly, and how would the answer move if it were a percent of the tag instead?

variant.prompt: Suppose one unit costs 12 dollars to make and the tag price is the cost plus a markup of 25 percent of that cost. What does the tag say?

problems.prompt: Peak 3 summit. Suppose making 5 units uses 8 meters of ribbon, every unit uses the same amount, and ribbon costs 3 dollars a meter. Suppose a tag reads 12 dollars, and late in the day every tag is cut by 25 percent. One unit sells at the cut price. How much of that money is left after paying for the ribbon that went into it?
explanation: Two separate questions are tangled together here, so do them one at a time and keep their numbers apart.
The ribbon first. Eight meters shared between 5 units is 1.6 meters inside each unit, and 1.6 meters at 3 dollars a meter costs 4.80 dollars.
Now the price. A cut of 25 percent takes away a quarter of the tag, and a quarter of 12 dollars is 3 dollars, so the cut price is 9.00 dollars.
What is left is the cut price less the ribbon inside that unit: 9.00 less 4.80 is 4.20 dollars.
The trap is cutting the wrong number. The 25 percent belongs to the tag, and the ribbon cost does not fall just because the price did.
problems.useAgain: when one sale has to be judged on its own and both the price and the cost inside it need working out first.
hints: There are two questions tangled together here. Work out what the ribbon in one unit costs before you look at the tag at all.
For the price, find a quarter of the tag and take it away, then compare what is left with the ribbon cost.
problems.socraticHint: When the tag price is cut, does the ribbon inside that unit get any cheaper?

variant.prompt: Suppose making 4 units uses 6 meters of ribbon, every unit uses the same amount, and ribbon costs 3 dollars a meter. A tag reads 14 dollars and late in the day every tag is cut by 50 percent. One unit sells at the cut price. How much of that money is left after paying for the ribbon that went into it?

problems.prompt: The month 2 monster gets its ending today, cracked or retired with honours: the token shop. A shop sells tokens worth 3 and 5 only, and you may buy as many of each as you like. Some exact amounts can never be paid with those tokens. Find every amount that can never be paid, and then prove the list is complete, which means showing that every amount you left off it really can be paid.

mustMention: the amounts that can never be paid are 1, 2, 4 and 7
every larger amount is one 3 token more than an amount already paid
so nothing above 7 is ever impossible

explanation: Start by paying what you can and writing it down. One token pays 3 or 5. Two tokens pay 6, 8 or 10. Three tokens pay 9, 11, 13 or 15.

Now sweep the small amounts in order: 1 no, 2 no, 3 yes, 4 no, 5 yes, 6 yes as two 3s, 7 no, 8 yes as a 3 and a 5, 9 yes as three 3s, 10 yes as two 5s. So the impossible ones found so far are 1, 2, 4 and 7.

Finding four is not the same as proving there are only four. The hard half of the monster is showing that nothing bigger ever fails, and no amount of checking by hand can show that, because the amounts never run out.

Here is the move that does it. Look at 8, 9 and 10: three amounts standing in a row, all payable. Take any amount of 11 or more and subtract 3. What is left is 8 or more, and it is smaller, so it has already been settled as payable.

So every amount from 11 up is paid by taking the way to pay the amount three below it and adding one more 3 token. Each amount is knocked over by the one three below it, and the line of falling never stops, so it reaches every amount forever. The impossible list ends at 7, and it is exactly 1, 2, 4 and 7.
One thing worth keeping. With a 3 token in your hand, three payable amounts in a row reach everything above them. A run of only two would not have been enough.
problems.useAgain: when a list of impossible cases has to be proved complete, and a run of successes in a row can be made to reach forever.
hints: Do not guess at the pattern. Take the amounts in order from 1 upwards and write yes or no beside each one, with the tokens that pay it whenever the answer is yes.
Once the noes seem to have stopped, look at the run of yeses at the end of your list. How many in a row have you got, and what does holding a 3 token let you do with a run that long?
problems.socraticHint: If you already knew that some amount could be paid, what is the easiest new amount you could pay without thinking at all?

variant.prompt: Same shop, different tokens: now it sells tokens worth 4 and 7 only. Which exact amounts can never be paid, and how do you know your list is complete?

mustMention: the amounts that can never be paid are 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 13 and 17
every larger amount is one 4 token more than an amount already paid

steps.title: Explain it
steps.prompt:
Write the crack of the token shop for a friend who has never seen it, one idea per sentence. Start with the sweep: the amounts in order from 1 upwards, with yes or no beside each, and the tokens that pay the yeses. Then say plainly that finding four impossible amounts is not yet a proof, because the amounts never run out and hands do.

Then the move that finishes it: three payable amounts standing in a row, and a 3 token that carries any of them forward. Explain why every amount above the run gets reached, and say what would have gone wrong if only two payable amounts in a row had turned up.

Put the list at the end, not the beginning, so your friend arrives at it the way you did.
